source.title: Human insula activation reflects risk prediction errors as well as risk.

confidence_rationale: Direct evidence that a region in the aversive/interoceptive network (anterior insula) carries a second-order signal: the error in the predicted size of prediction errors (risk prediction error), separable from the first-order reward prediction error. That is the existence of an 'expected error' channel attached to a first-order predictor. Held at 0.5 and marked mixed because the task is a monetary gamble whose risk is purely aleatoric outcome variance with a known generative model; it does not show the brain estimating its OWN predictor's reliability or separating model error from world variance.
failure_signatures: Risk here is outcome variance of a known lottery (aleatoric), so a positive reading conflates 'expected squared error' with 'predictor competence'; MECH-585 needs the latter.
Reward gambling, not harm; transfer to the harm stream assumes insula's role is valence-general.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Early-onset anterior insula activation correlates with risk prediction error (the mismatch between predicted and realised squared reward prediction error); a later activation tracks risk prediction itself.
mapping.ree_translation: Biological precedent for ingredient (a) of MECH-585: a per-state expected-error estimate, updated by its own error signal, maintained alongside the first-order PE. Supports that a predicted magnitude can carry an associated, separately-learned expected-error term.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Expected error here is irreducible outcome variance, not calibrated model error of a learned forward model; nothing in the design lets the insula attribute error to 'my predictor is bad' versus 'the world is noisy'. No competence-floor analogue. Valence is reward, not harm.
mapping.source_context: fMRI, human card-gambling task with continuously changing reward probability and hence risk.

confidence_components.notes: Well-cited, model-based fMRI; mapping is to the expected-error representation only, not to the attribution the claim asserts.
